title: Grids & Grid-and-Compute
summary:
The grid is the part of the energy system that has quietly become *the* binding constraint — and it's the specialism you're building toward, so it's worth understanding deeply. Generation gets cheaper every year, but you can't use a megawatt you can't deliver, and you can't connect a project the grid can't host. Whoever understands grid constraints understands where value and risk actually sit.

Start with the **actors and layers**. The **TSO (Transmission System Operator)** — TenneT in the Netherlands and much of Germany — runs the high-voltage backbone, keeps supply and demand balanced in real time, and maintains **frequency** (50 Hz in Europe) and system security. The **DSO (Distribution System Operator)** runs the lower-voltage local networks that deliver power to homes and businesses. Transmission moves bulk power long distances at high voltage to cut losses; distribution is the last-mile delivery. Increasingly, **HVDC** links (efficient over long distances and for sub-sea interconnectors) complement the AC grid.

Keeping the system stable is a constant balancing act. Frequency must stay near 50 Hz; deviations are arrested and restored by the reserve products from pm01 (**FCR, aFRR, mFRR**). **Inertia** from spinning synchronous machines slows frequency swings, and as those plants retire the grid leans on faster reserves and grid-forming inverters (see et01). The network is planned to the **N-1 security criterion**: it must survive the loss of any single element without cascading. When the cheapest dispatch would overload a line, the TSO intervenes with **redispatch** — paying one plant down and another up to relieve **congestion**. The cost of that congestion management has exploded as renewables are often far from demand.

Congestion is also where markets and physics meet. Europe mostly uses **zonal pricing** (one price per bidding zone, congestion handled out-of-market via redispatch); some systems use **nodal pricing / LMPs** (a price at every grid node that reflects local congestion directly). Cross-border capacity is shared via **flow-based market coupling**. The recurring theme: the grid, not generation, increasingly sets what's possible — hence multi-year **connection queues** for both new renewables and new loads.

That brings the frontier: **grid-and-compute**. AI and cloud data centres are enormous, fast-growing, and unusually **flexible** electrical loads, and they can sometimes be sited freely. That makes them a grid variable, not just a consumer. The emerging thesis — central to roles at TSOs and players like DNV and Northpool — is to **site compute where the grid and the renewable resource have headroom**, **co-locate** data centres with generation (behind-the-meter or near substations with spare capacity), and use their flexibility (shifting non-urgent compute, curtailing, or providing demand response) to *help* balance the system rather than strain it. Done well, a data centre becomes firming demand that monetises otherwise-curtailed renewables; done badly, it's a connection-queue-jamming peak that forces grid reinforcement. Reading which is which — connection capacity, congestion maps, flexibility value — is exactly the analyst skill this track is building.

equations.name: Load factor
equations.useWhen: Judging how 'peaky' a load or system is. A high load factor (flat, steady demand) uses grid and generation capacity efficiently; a low one means expensive capacity sits idle most of the time.
equations.note: Data centres have a very high load factor (~0.9+) — steady, around-the-clock demand — which is part of what makes them attractive *and* heavy on the grid.

equations.name: Energy from power over time
equations.useWhen: Converting a steady load or generation in MW to energy in MWh over a period — e.g. the daily energy a constant data-centre load draws.
equations.note: The same relation used to size storage duration in et01. For varying power, use the average over the period.

glossary.definition: Operator of the high-voltage backbone (e.g. TenneT). Balances supply and demand in real time, maintains frequency and security, and procures reserves. The system's air-traffic control.
Operator of the lower-voltage local networks delivering power to end users. Increasingly active as rooftop solar, EVs and heat pumps make distribution two-way.
Transmission = bulk power over long distances at high voltage (low losses); distribution = local last-mile delivery at lower voltage. Different operators, voltages and roles.
High-voltage AC is the default grid; high-voltage DC is more efficient over long distances and essential for sub-sea interconnectors and tying asynchronous grids together.
The European grid runs at 50 Hz; frequency rises if generation exceeds demand and falls if demand exceeds generation. Keeping it near 50 Hz is continuous real-time balancing.
Rotational energy in synchronous machines that slows frequency changes, buying time for reserves to act. Declines as renewables replace spinning plants. (See et01.)
When the economically cheapest power flows would overload a transmission element. The grid bottleneck that forces market or operational intervention.
The TSO paying one generator to reduce output and another (the 'wrong' side of a constraint) to increase it, to relieve congestion. Its cost has risen sharply with remote renewables.
The grid must withstand the loss of any single component (line, transformer, generator) without cascading failure. The core reliability standard driving spare capacity.
One wholesale price per bidding zone; internal congestion is handled outside the market via redispatch. The European norm. (Contrast nodal.) (See pm01.)
A locational marginal price at every grid node, directly reflecting local congestion and losses. Used in much of the US; sends sharp siting signals but is complex.
The method coupling European zones that allocates cross-border capacity using the physics of power flows, rather than simple fixed transfer limits.
The multi-year backlog of generation *and* load projects waiting for grid capacity and permission to connect. Now a primary constraint on both renewables and data centres.
The technical rules a connecting asset must meet (voltage ride-through, frequency response, reactive power). Increasingly demands grid-supporting behaviour from renewables and loads.
Power that does no net work but is needed to sustain grid voltage. An ancillary service the TSO procures; inverters and synchronous condensers can provide it.
Average load ÷ peak load. High (flat) load factor uses capacity efficiently; low (peaky) load means costly capacity sits idle much of the time.
The system's maximum instantaneous load, which transmission and generation must be built to meet (with N-1 margin) even if it occurs only a few hours a year.
The system's ability to adjust supply, demand or flows to handle variability and constraints — from storage, flexible generation, demand response and smart grid controls.
Loads that can shift, shed or modulate consumption — EV charging, heat pumps, industry and data centres. A growing grid resource and the heart of grid-and-compute.
Generation or storage on the customer's side of the grid connection (e.g. a solar array or battery serving an on-site data centre), reducing or reshaping the grid demand.
Siting a large load (like a data centre) directly with generation or at a substation with spare capacity, cutting transmission need and connection delay.
The thesis of siting and operating data-centre/AI load as a grid-aware, flexible resource — placed where grid and renewable headroom exist, helping balance rather than strain the system.
Large, fast-growing, around-the-clock electricity demand from AI/cloud computing. Often siteable and partly flexible, making it a grid variable, not just a consumer.
A grid with digital sensing, communication and control that enables real-time visibility, demand response and active management of distributed resources.
Restarting the grid from a full blackout using units that can energise without external supply (hydro, diesel, increasingly batteries). A key resilience service. (See et01.)

tips: **The grid is the bottleneck, not generation.** Connection queues and congestion — not turbine cost — increasingly decide what gets built and where. Lead grid analysis with capacity and constraints.
**Know the TSO/DSO split.** TSO (TenneT) = high-voltage backbone, balancing, frequency, security; DSO = local distribution. Most balancing and interconnection questions are TSO-level.
**Redispatch cost is the price of congestion.** Rising redispatch spend signals that generation has outrun the wires — an argument for grid build-out, storage, or siting load near supply.
**Zonal vs nodal = how congestion is priced.** Zonal (Europe) hides it inside a zone and fixes it via redispatch; nodal (US LMP) prices it at every node and signals siting directly.

**Data centres are a grid variable, not just a load.** Siteable, flexible, high-load-factor demand can monetise curtailed renewables and provide demand response — *or* jam queues and force reinforcement. The analysis is which.
**Load factor reveals how hard capacity works.** A high load factor (steady demand, like a data centre) uses expensive grid and generation capacity efficiently; peaky load wastes it.
